content: 1. The HIV/AIDS Surveillance Project in Pakistan introduced an innovative mapping approach to estimate the size and distribution of high-risk groups for HIV. This method was detailed in a publication accessed on August 30, 2016. 2. UNAIDS released an issue brief in 2014 focusing on local HIV epidemics, providing resources and strategies for addressing these challenges. This document was accessed on November 16, 2016. 3. K4Health developed a toolkit in 2016 titled Tools Together Now, which includes 100 participatory tools designed to mobilize communities for HIV/AIDS prevention and care. This resource was accessed on August 4, 2016. 4. Aronson and colleagues proposed an ethnographically informed community evaluation framework in 2007, which provides a structured approach to assess community-based health initiatives. 5. Spradley’s 1980 work on participant observation remains a foundational text for ethnographic research methodologies. 6. Guest, Bunce, and Johnson conducted a 2006 study to determine the number of interviews required to achieve data saturation and variability in qualitative research. 7. Grimes and Schulz discussed the utility of cohort studies in achieving outcome-based research in a Lancet publication. 8. The Melbourne Injecting Drug User Cohort Study (MIX), established by Horyniak et al. in 2013, provided insights into the rationale, methods, and outcomes of a 12-month follow-up study on harm reduction. 9. Yang and colleagues investigated HIV incidence and associated factors among men who have sex with men in Nanjing, China, in a 2010 study published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 10. Shah et al. explored sexual risk behaviors and HIV prevalence among clients and partners of female sex workers in Bangkok, Thailand, in a 2011 study published in the Journal of Urban Health. 11. Data documentation involves maintaining a detailed record of how data are collected, defined, organized, processed, and analyzed. This includes steps like cleaning, error checking, and variable creation. 12. A data dictionary or codebook describes the content of a dataset, including valid ranges, logic checks, and skip patterns. Many systems can automatically generate these resources. 13. A data management plan is essential for ensuring high-quality data collection. It includes components such as data documentation, data dictionaries, unique participant identifiers, data-quality checks, skip patterns, data entry protocols, confidentiality measures, access guidelines, backup strategies, and archiving/version control. 14. Unique participant identifiers are critical for linking all collected data to a specific individual while preventing reuse or errors. Barcodes and preprinted labels can reduce transcription errors. 15. Data-quality checks are integral to the data collection process, helping to prevent data loss and minimize errors. Validation rules and skip patterns should be developed before data collection begins. 16. Data entry errors can significantly impact analysis. Double data entry is recommended for paper-based questionnaires to ensure accuracy, despite its higher cost. 17. Data confidentiality protects against unauthorized access, particularly to participants' identities. Surveys should be conducted anonymously, or measures must be implemented to ensure confidentiality and security. 18. Guidelines for data access and use should define who can access data, who owns it, and how it will be used. Data analysis should only be conducted on de-identified datasets. 19. Data backup is crucial to prevent loss due to hardware/software failures, viruses, or human error. Automated backup systems are ideal, and backups should be verified regularly. 20. Data archiving and version control ensure that all versions of a dataset are preserved and managed systematically. Changes should be supervised and documented according to the data management plan. 21. Data security and storage require safeguards to prevent accidental or malicious disclosure. This includes using passwords, encryption, and secure storage for both paper-based and electronic data. 22. During data transmission, secure methods such as virtual private networks (VPNs) should be used to prevent unauthorized access. Data should never be transmitted over unsecured Wi-Fi or internet connections.
